title: Pathway to Redwood: Adapter & Parity Demo
next_steps: Send parity-matrix.csv with example mappings and cost estimates
Schedule 1-week pilot to run 100k tokens through Redwood Dedicated pool
Share SOC2 and network architecture docs (VPC options)
action_items: Maya Chen: email parity-matrix.csv and pricing snapshot by 2026-02-07
Diego Alvarez: provision a sandbox account and upload sample prompt set by 2026-02-10
Ravi Singh: provide a list of peak qps and current batch sizes by 2026-02-09
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Cobalt through adapter-based migration approach for switching endpoints from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to the Redwood API. Demo covered parity mapping rules, console routing, Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization, and private deployment options. Customer raised latency vs. cost concerns and SOC2/KMS questions. Agreed next steps include parity matrix share, sandbox provisioning, and a short pilot run.
transcript:
Header: 2026-02-05 17:00 UTC | Duration: 38m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez (Redwood); Jill Park, Ravi Singh, Lina Morales (Cobalt)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Quick agenda — we want to show a pragmatic adapter approach to move your OpenAI/Anthropic endpoints over to Redwood with parity mapping and cost/latency tradeoffs. Diego will demo the console and Optimize tips.

[00:22] Jill Park: Hi Maya, hi Diego. Quick context: we're running a mixed stack, mostly OpenAI for chat, Anthropic for some assistant flows, and a few Together models for internal embeddings. Main asks: keep latency under 120ms p50, and not blow up costs. Also Lina will ask security questions.

[00:40] Diego Alvarez: Cool. We'll start with mapping. The easiest path is an adapter layer that translates your current request shapes to Redwood API calls. So for OpenAI completions you map model name -> redwood-compat model, keep messages structure, and we support streaming and tool/function calls. For Anthropic we map role tokens and temp settings. For Together, embeddings map one-to-one to our embeddings endpoint.

[01:12] Ravi Singh: When you say "redwood-compat model" is that a 1:1 parity or a closest-match? We have prompt-optimized models and a lot of safety tuning.

[01:25] Diego Alvarez: Good question. It's closest-match; we provide a parity-matrix with recommended vendor->Redwood model mappings and expected delta on latency and token quality. For edge cases we can run an eval on your prompt set. We'll include quantization recommendations if you need lower cost.

[01:48] Jill Park: Can you show the console mapping UI? I want to see how painless that is for product teams.

[02:05] Diego Alvarez: Sure, sharing screen. Pulling up Redwood Console -> Projects -> Parity mappings.

[02:15] (screen share noise)

[02:24] Diego Alvarez: Here you can upload a CSV or use the UI to map vendor_model -> redwood_model, set fallback model tiers, and apply routing policies by route or env. Example: openai/gpt-4o -> redwood/gpt4o-1. We also show estimated cost delta per 1M tokens and an estimated p50 token latency. Those estimates come from our benchmark catalog.

[03:05] Jill Park: I see a "fallback" column — does that trigger automatic fallback if the primary model is out of capacity?

[03:12] Diego Alvarez: Yes. Policy-based routing — primary, then cheaper dedicated variant, then hosted best-effort. You can also pin by customer or route.

[03:40] Lina Morales: Security — how do you handle data residency and KMS? We need encrypt-at-rest and audit logs for any private deployment.

[03:53] Maya Chen: We support VPC/private control plane, HSM integrations, and customer-managed KMS. Audit logs and token-level tracing are available in the Console and can be exported for retention. We'll share our SOC2 and architecture docs after the call.

[04:12] Lina Morales: And SSO? SAML?

[04:18] Diego Alvarez: Yes, SAML SSO + RBAC. We can also provision a dedicated tenant for you if you go Private.

[04:36] Ravi Singh: Back to performance — you mentioned batching and KV caching. How much do we need to change on our side?

[04:45] Diego Alvarez: Minimal. For batching, you can keep your same request rate, and our SDK adds an optional batching middleware. For KV cache (we sometimes see docs show "K V cash" in transcriptions), you only need to pass the conversation key. Automatic prefix caching reduces token compute for repeated context. Optimize will analyze your traffic and suggest batch sizes and quantization profiles—usually we see 20-40% cost reduction with negligible latency impact for chat workloads.

[05:24] Jill Park: Can you quantify that with an example for our use case? We do a lot of short-turn chat (avg prompt 40 tokens, response 80 tokens).

[05:36] Diego Alvarez: With those numbers, moving from a 16-bit to an 8-bit quantized variant plus batching at qps bursts we estimate 25-35% cost savings and p50 impact of ~10-20ms depending on your infra. We'll put numbers in the parity-matrix.csv.

[06:05] Jill Park: What's the ramp plan? We're worried about regressions.

[06:12] Maya Chen: Typical plan: 1) import parity mappings and run a smoke pilot on a subset of routes, 2) run parallel A/B with canary traffic (10-30%), 3) run evals on your golden prompt sets using our eval harness, 4) full cutover with rollback policies. Diego will help set up the canary and tracing hooks.

[06:38] Ravi Singh: For the pilot, do you support the same metrics we use? We track p50/p95, cost per 1k tokens, and hallucination rate via our internal checks.

[06:50] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we export p50/p95 and token-level cost. For hallucination detection we have a lightweight eval integration you can run against a stored prompt set. We'll also wire your telemetry to our Console via tracing hooks.

[07:12] (pause)

[07:20] Diego Alvarez: Now I'll flip to Optimize. This is a small part of Console that ingests your call distribution and recommends batching, cache TTLs, and whether a quantized model is a good fit.

[07:35] (clicking)

[07:40] Diego Alvarez: Example: if you have lots of short responses, we recommend small batch windows (20-50ms) plus aggressive prefix caching. Optimize shows expected token cost delta and a compatibility score.

[08:05] Jill Park: Are these recommendations auto-applied or just suggestions?

[08:11] Diego Alvarez: Suggestions by default. You can enable automated policies, e.g., auto-batch under defined latency SLOs. We rarely recommend automatic quantization without a manual eval step.

[08:30] Lina Morales: How do you handle PII in logs when we run pilots?

[08:36] Maya Chen: You can mask or redact at the SDK layer. If on Private, you can disable retention entirely. In Hosted we have retention controls and encrypted logs with customer-managed keys for enterprise customers.

[09:00] Jill Park: Can we run a short benchmark here live — maybe a small set of prompts — to see p50?

[09:06] Diego Alvarez: Yes, let's run your top 5 prompts. Ravi, can you paste the example prompt set in the chat?

[09:18] Ravi Singh: Pasting now. (chat noise)

[09:28] Diego Alvarez: Running through the demo harness. We're sending requests to a redwood-compat model that mimics your OpenAI profile. Live p50: 110ms, p95: 260ms for this small sample. That's on par with your SLA target.

[09:55] Jill Park: Nice. How would Dedicated behave if we had predictable throughput?

[10:02] Diego Alvarez: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, lower variance on p95, and predictable unit economics. You trade off higher baseline commit for lower per-token costs. We can show a cost model in the parity-matrix.

[10:22] Ravi Singh: Any hidden infra changes? Our infra team is sensitive to network egress and VPC peering.

[10:29] Maya Chen: For Private/VPC we do peering via customer-managed transit. For Hosted, egress is standard cloud egress; the console shows region routing and you can pin requests to regions to minimize egress. We'll provide network diagrams.

[10:50] (small technical deep-dive prompt)

[11:00] Diego Alvarez: Quick note on function/tool calling: we support both OpenAI-style function call semantics and structured outputs. You can map calls and we surface debug traces in Console. For Anthropic tool patterns we map role-based sequences.

[11:28] Jill Park: About Together embeddings — we use them for semantic search. Any migration gotchas there?

[11:36] Diego Alvarez: Embeddings are usually straight 1:1. The caveat is dimension sizes and normalization differences. Optimize will recommend reindexing thresholds. We can run vector similarity checks against a sample to confirm recall.

[12:05] Ravi Singh: Who owns the rollout? Our platform team or Redwood?

[12:12] Maya Chen: It's collaborative. Redwood SEs will help set up the canary and provide the console dashboards; your platform team triggers the ramp and owns traffic. We provide runbooks and rollback steps.

[12:32] Lina Morales: On audit logs, can we get per-request user attribution and masked payload?

[12:40] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we have per-request metadata and the option to redact content fields. For private customers we can retain logs in your storage and disable retention in our plane.

[12:58] Jill Park: Ok, pricing is the elephant. Can you share a simple cost delta for our 1M token incremental?

[13:08] Diego Alvarez: Roughly: hosted comparable model ~ $X/1k tokens, quantized dedicated variant ~ 20-30% cheaper after commit. We'll surface exact pricing in the parity matrix; depends on commit level and batch patterns.

[13:35] (some cross talk and interruptions)

[14:00] Diego Alvarez: A couple product caveats — streaming vs non-streaming affects latency numbers. If you stream token-by-token there's an extra scheduling overhead, but users see earlier increments. For strict p50 you'd want short-stream windows or partial streaming.

[14:20] Jill Park: Any SDK changes for streaming?

[14:28] Diego Alvarez: Minimal. Our SDK mirrors OpenAI streaming interfaces. You can swap out endpoints and keep your client logic mostly intact.

[15:00] Ravi Singh: Let's talk failure modes. If a model throws 502s under load, what's Redwood's fallback?

[15:08] Maya Chen: Automatic fallback to the next policy tier, and we surface errors in Console and can trigger automated alerting. For Dedicated we have capacity autoscaling policies and burst windows.

[15:30] Jill Park: For the pilot, we need a guarantee around data isolation. How is that documented?

[15:38] Maya Chen: We'll send our Private deployment whitepaper and the SOC2 package. We'll also include a proposed network diagram for your security review.

[15:50] (brief pause)

[16:05] Diego Alvarez: Demo wrap — provisioning. Diego: I'll provision a sandbox project and upload the parity-matrix.csv with the mappings we discussed. You'll get an invite to the Console and the sample canary script.

[16:22] Jill Park: That sounds good. Two other items: 1) we need to validate hallucination metrics, 2) can you show how to configure rollback thresholds in Console?

[16:33] Diego Alvarez: Yes, the eval harness will generate hallucination metrics against your golden set. Rollback thresholds are in the Deployments -> Policies tab; you can set p95 or error-rate thresholds to auto-rollback.

[16:58] Ravi Singh: Any compliance red flags for us moving from Anthropic to Redwood?

[17:05] Maya Chen: Not from our side. We can do a security review session with Lina and your SREs. We'll bring our security engineer to that call.

[17:20] (questions from Lina about retention windows and KMS integration specifics)

[17:40] Maya Chen: We'll include a KMS integration guide; short answer: you can bring your key to Private or use CMK in hosted with HSM backends for enterprise.

[18:02] Jill Park: Time check — we're at 18 minutes. Any remaining items?

[18:08] Diego Alvarez: I'm going to quickly show the parity CSV example in the chat link: https://redwood.example.com/shared/parity-matrix.csv — it'll contain recommended model mappings, expected cost delta, and suggested quantization pockets.

[18:25] Jill Park: Perfect. If we agree on the pilot, what is the timeline?

[18:32] Maya Chen: Typical turnaround: parity matrix + sandbox in 48-72 hours, pilot runs 1-2 weeks to capture variance, then review and decide full migration.

[18:46] Ravi Singh: Good. Lina, any more security questions?

[18:51] Lina Morales: We'll need to review the SOC2 docs and the KMS integration guide. Also would like an SLA draft.

[18:59] Maya Chen: We'll attach those to the follow-up email.

[19:05] (wrap-up)

[19:12] Maya Chen: Quick recap: share parity-matrix.csv and pilot pricing; Redwood to provision sandbox and canary; security docs + SOC2 and KMS guide; schedule security review. Next call: provision complete -> pilot kickoff sync on 2026-02-11.

[19:30] Jill Park: Thanks all. Looking forward to the parity CSV.

[19:36] Diego Alvarez: Thanks, we'll follow up.

[19:40] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcription includes occasional mis-hearings, e.g., "K V cash" for KV cache; timestamps are approximate. Shared artifacts mentioned: parity-matrix.csv (link above), sandbox invite, SOC2 packet.
